pillars.name: Operational Excellence
pillars.summary: Build software correctly and keep delivering a great customer experience. Automate safely, make small reversible changes, observe everything and learn from failure.

pillars.name: Security
pillars.summary: Protect data, systems and assets with strong identity and least privilege, traceability, encryption in transit and at rest, and defence in depth.

pillars.name: Reliability
pillars.summary: A reliable workload does its intended job correctly and consistently. It recovers from failure automatically, scales horizontally and has no single point of failure.

pillars.name: Performance Efficiency
pillars.summary: Use computing resources efficiently to meet requirements, even as demand changes. Pick the right resource types, go global in minutes, and prefer managed and serverless services.

pillars.name: Cost Optimization
pillars.summary: Deliver business value at the lowest price point. Pay only for what you use, right-size, measure spend and stop paying for idle resources.

pillars.name: Sustainability
pillars.summary: Minimise the environmental impact of running cloud workloads. Keep utilisation high, use managed services, and store and move less data.

puzzles.title: Thumbnail Factory
puzzles.story: The city photo club uploads hundreds of pictures a day and wants a small thumbnail of each one created automatically. Traffic is spiky: quiet all week, flooded after events.
requirements: Store original photos durably
Create a thumbnail automatically whenever a photo is uploaded
Pay nothing for compute when nobody is uploading
puzzles.why: An S3 event notification invokes a Lambda function on each upload. The function resizes the image and writes the thumbnail to a separate bucket or prefix. Never write back to the source prefix, or each thumbnail triggers the function again in a recursive loop. Lambda scales with uploads and costs nothing when idle, unlike an always-on EC2 server.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Each upload wakes Lambda to make a small copy, saved somewhere else so it doesn't loop forever. No uploads, no bill.

reference.title: Tutorial: Using an Amazon S3 trigger to create thumbnail images

operational.tip: Alarm on Lambda errors and duration so you notice failed thumbnails before users do.

security.tip: Give the function a role that can only read the source prefix and write the thumbnail prefix.

reliability.tip: Buffer events through SQS with a dead-letter queue so bursts and bad images are retried or isolated.

performance.tip: Tune Lambda memory: more memory also means more CPU, often making image resizing faster.

cost.tip: Lambda costs nothing between uploads; S3 lifecycle rules move old originals to cheaper storage classes.

sustainability.tip: Event-driven compute runs only when there is work, so no servers sit idle burning energy.

puzzles.story: The city library app lets members sign in and save their reading lists. Only signed-in members may call the API, and each member must only see their own list.

puzzles.title: Market Day Orders
puzzles.story: On market day the bakery gets thousands of orders in minutes. The order API must never drop an order, even if the back office is slow or a bad order breaks processing.
requirements: Accept orders instantly through an API
Buffer orders so processing can catch up
Retry failures and isolate orders that keep failing
Store processed orders durably
puzzles.why: API Gateway writes each order to an SQS queue and returns immediately, so customers never wait on processing. Lambda polls the queue in batches and writes to DynamoDB. Messages that fail repeatedly move to a dead-letter queue instead of blocking the line. Standard queues deliver each message at least once, so make processing idempotent (safe to run twice).
puzzles.simpleWhy: Orders wait in a queue, so customers never wait. Lambda works through them, and broken ones are set aside instead of blocking the line.

performance.tip: Lambda scales pollers with queue depth; tune batch size and use partial batch responses.

puzzles.title: Two-Continent Booking System
puzzles.story: The city's hotel booking service now has guests in Europe and North America. It must stay fast for both and keep working if an entire AWS Region has problems.
requirements: Low-latency reads for users on both continents
Data replicated to a second Region
Traffic moves to the healthy Region automatically
Recovery without manual database rebuilds
puzzles.why: DynamoDB global tables keep multi-active replicas in each Region, so apps read and write locally. By default they use eventual consistency (MREC), where the last write wins, so two Regions could book the same room at once. To prevent that, create the table with multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC), or send each hotel's bookings to one home Region. MRSC uses exactly three Regions: three replicas, or two replicas and a witness. Route 53 latency routing with health checks sends users to the lowest-latency healthy Region. Failover routing is the alternative: it sends users to a standby Region when the primary fails. For relational data, Aurora Global Database has one writer Region and low-lag read replicas in others. It offers a managed cross-Region failover that you start, and that typically completes within minutes. ElastiCache Global Datastore can add a cross-Region cache for faster reads. It is a cache, not the booking system of record, and you promote its Region manually.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Copies of the bookings live on both continents, so everyone books nearby. Careful rules stop two people booking the same room.

operational.tip: Monitor replication latency and rehearse Region failover regularly (game days).

security.tip: Encrypt replicas with keys in each Region and keep IAM policies consistent across Regions.

reliability.tip: Multi-Region data plus health-checked DNS failover removes the Region as a single point of failure. With MRSC, a Region failover loses no confirmed bookings.

puzzles.title: Every New Account, Ready
puzzles.story: The council gives each team its own AWS account. Every new account must get the same audit trail on day one, all the trails must keep their logs in one central bucket, and no team may ever switch its trail off.
requirements: Create team accounts and group them by ward
Set up the same audit trail in every new account
Keep every account's logs in one central bucket
Stop anyone in a team account turning the trail off
puzzles.why: AWS Organizations groups the team accounts into OUs. A CloudFormation StackSet with service-managed permissions targets those OUs, and with automatic deployment turned on it builds the baseline stack, including a CloudTrail trail, in every account that joins. The trails deliver their logs to one central S3 bucket in a log archive account. A service control policy on the team OUs denies stopping or deleting the trail, so no team can switch it off.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Orla groups the accounts, Forma builds the same setup in each new one, and a by-law stops anyone switching the record off.

reference.title: Organizing Your AWS Environment Using Multiple Accounts

operational.tip: Change the baseline in one template, and StackSets rolls the change out to every account.

security.tip: Give each team its own account, and fence each ward with an SCP that keeps the trail on.

reliability.tip: Deploy the baseline automatically, never by hand, so no new account is ever missed.

performance.tip: S3 holds years of logs from every account, with no servers or disks to size.

puzzles.title: Sports Day Live
puzzles.story: On sports day, judges post scores from their phones and thousands of families watch the results board update live. Only signed-in judges may post scores; everyone else just watches.
requirements: Judges sign in before posting scores
Post and read scores through one endpoint
Push every new score to watching phones at once
Keep scores in a serverless database
puzzles.why: Judges sign in with an Amazon Cognito user pool, and AppSync checks their token before any mutation runs; families read through a second authorization mode, such as IAM or an API key. A resolver saves each score to DynamoDB. Because AppSync subscriptions are triggered by mutations, the new score is pushed over WebSockets to every phone that subscribed, with no polling.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Coco checks the judges, Gracie saves each score in the library and rings every watching phone at once.

reference.title: Using subscriptions for real-time data applications in AWS AppSync

operational.tip: Turn on AppSync's logs and metrics, so a slow resolver shows up on the day.

security.tip: Only signed-in judges may run mutations; families get read-only access.

reliability.tip: DynamoDB keeps the scores in several Availability Zones, so the board survives one going dark.
